item.title: Awa Odori: Japan's Greatest Dance Festival — Guide
item.description: Awa Odori is the most famous dance festival in Japan and the pride of Tokushima, held each year during the mid-August Obon season and drawing well over a million spectators. Over four days and nights, the streets of Tokushima city fill with ‘ren’ — dance troupes of choreographed performers, some over a hundred strong — parading and dancing to the driving, hypnotic rhythm of taiko drums, shamisen, flutes and bells. The dance has a distinctive loose, flowing style, with dancers in colourful yukata and the women in half-moon straw hats, all chanting the famous refrain: ‘the dancing fool and the watching fool are both fools, so you might as well dance!

item.title: Uwajima Toro Nagashi Lantern Floating — Guide
item.description: Toro nagashi is a gentle, deeply moving Japanese tradition held during the Obon season in summer, when the spirits of ancestors are believed to return and then depart again. In Uwajima on Ehime’s southern coast, glowing paper lanterns — each carrying a candle and often a prayer or the name of a departed loved one — are set adrift on the water at dusk, floating out across the bay in a slow, shimmering procession of light to guide the souls of the dead peacefully back to the other world.

item.title: Koyasan Candle Festival: 100,000 Lights Along Okunoin — Guide
item.description: The Koyasan Candle Festival (Rosoku Matsuri), held on the evening of August 13th at the start of Obon, is one of Japan’s most moving summer sights. Along the entire two-kilometre approach to Okunoin, from Ichinohashi bridge to Kobo Daishi’s mausoleum, some 100,000 candles are set out and lit by visitors and pilgrims, so that the path through the ancient cedars becomes a shimmering river of small flames winding between 200,000 tombs.

item.title: Aizu-Wakamatsu Lantern Festival: A Summer Obon Tradition — Guide
item.description: The Aizu-Wakamatsu Lantern Festival takes place during the Obon season in August, when thousands of paper lanterns are lit along the city’s historic streets and around Tsurugajo Castle to honour ancestral spirits, a Buddhist tradition observed across Japan but given a particularly atmospheric setting here. As dusk falls, the warm glow of the lanterns against the castle backdrop and old townscape creates one of Fukushima’s most photogenic summer scenes, accompanied by traditional bon-odori folk dancing in the streets.

item.title: Eisa Guide: Okinawa's Drum Dance, Festivals & Where to See It
item.description: Eisa is Okinawa’s electrifying traditional drum-and-dance — rows of performers in vivid costume pounding taiko drums and spinning to the call of the sanshin, all driven by a hypnotic chant and whistle. Rooted in Obon ceremonies to honour ancestral spirits, eisa has grown into a proud symbol of Okinawan identity performed at festivals, cultural parks and street events. The spectacular Okinawa Zento (“All-Island”) Eisa Festival in Okinawa City each autumn is the grandest gathering of all.
